(i) the use of fully-digital precoders and postcoders is in general the best choice in terms of energy efficiency, and that (ii) the use of hybrid structures, based on the exclusive employment of switches, is in general not a good option, since it leads to a significant performance loss.

(i) fully-digital beamforming is not always energy efficient, (ii) hybrid beamforming with a large number RF chains at the transmitter is not energy efficient, (iii) hybrid beamforming using switches at the transmitter is very inefficient, and (iv) hybrid beamforming is not necessarily more energy efficient than fully-digital beamfoming.

(i) the fully digital structure is energy efficient in the case of large antenna arrays and low SNR, (ii) the hybrid structures based on phase shifters and a small number of RF chains (e.g. 2 or 4) are energy efficient in the high SNR regime, and (iii) the hybrid structures with a large number (>4) of RF chains are energy efficient in all the SNR regimes.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the energy efficiency of the fully digital beamforming structure is the best, followed by hybrid beamformers with phase shifters, and finally by hybrid beamforming structures based on switches.

The main takeaway from our work is that
a careful analysis of both the energy efficiency and the spectral efficiency of different structures is necessary before selecting a beamforming architecture for mmWave systems.
the use of switches for beamforming in mmWave cellular networks may not be the most energy-efficient choice, and that the use of phase shifters may be more beneficial, at least for the downlink.

a careful analysis and design of low-complexity beamformers is needed to achieve a good performance, and that a simple switch-only beamforming structure should not be considered as a valid alternative to fully-digital beamforming in mmWave systems.
